transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Yeah, so, I guess I’m here because... well, it’s a bit hard to explain, but it’s been bothering me enough that I finally decided I needed to talk to someone about it. I work as a supervisor for a construction company, managing the trades and extraction crews mostly. It’s a lot of managing personalities, making sure safety protocols are followed, dealing with weather delays, supply chain stuff... you know, just high stress. 

And then, on top of being out on the site all day, I often have to attend these neighborhood association meetings in the evenings to explain to angry residents why we’re blocking their roads or making noise at six in the morning. So by the time I finally get home, I am just completely drained. Physically and mentally wiped out. 

And what made me finally bring this up and make an appointment is that after those really long days on site, or after a particularly bad neighborhood meeting, I’ll come home and I just... I eat way, way more than I ever meant to. I'll walk into the kitchen, kick my boots off, and it's like a switch flips. I’ll start with maybe some leftover takeout from the fridge, like cold noodles or whatever, and then I’ll move on to pouring myself massive bowls of cereal, then I'll find a bag of chips... really, just whatever’s there in the pantry. I just keep eating and eating until I’m so uncomfortably full, like my stomach is physically stretched and hurting. I just can't seem to stop myself when I get into that mode, and it's really starting to mess with my head.
Do you usually feel anxious, stressed, or upset right before these episodes of eating a lot?

Well, I mean... I guess I’m not entirely sure if anxious or upset is exactly the right word for what I’m feeling right in that specific moment before it happens. Like I was saying, the job itself is just incredibly stressful all the time. Just the other day, for example, we had this massive issue with a concrete delivery being delayed by three hours, which throws off the whole schedule, and then the trades are just sitting around on the clock doing nothing, and my boss is breathing down my neck... so yeah, my baseline is pretty much always stressed. And those neighborhood meetings, oh my gosh, people can be so incredibly mean about things I have absolutely zero control over, like the construction dust getting on their cars or the backup alarms on the trucks. 

But when I actually get home and walk into the kitchen... I don't know if I'm actively feeling upset right then. It’s more like... well, it’s hard to explain. Sometimes I’m not even thinking about the concrete or the angry neighbors anymore. I just walk in, and the house is quiet, and my feet are throbbing from being in steel-toe boots for fourteen hours, and my brain just sort of... flatlines? I haven't really noticed a specific emotional trigger right before I open the fridge, like I'm not standing there crying or having a panic attack or anything like that. It’s just this overwhelming sense of being totally depleted, and then before I even really process what I'm feeling or what kind of mood I'm in, I'm already eating. So, I don't know, maybe it is all that stress catching up to me, but I just haven't really been able to pinpoint exactly what's going through my head right before the eating starts. I just know it happens at the end of those really long days.
Do you usually feel guilty after these episodes of eating a lot?

Guilty... um, you know, I’m not sure if guilt is really the right word for it. I haven't really noticed feeling guilty, per se. I mean, when I think of guilt, I usually think of doing something wrong to someone else, you know? Like if I messed up a concrete pour on site and cost the client thousands of dollars, or if I snapped at one of my foremen when they didn't deserve it. But with this... it's not really like that. 

After I finish eating all that food—the leftover takeout, the cereal, the chips, just whatever I ended up grabbing—I’m usually just sitting there on my living room couch, and my stomach is so stretched out it practically aches. I'll be looking at the empty wrappers or the bowls sitting there on the coffee table, and it's not like I'm sitting there beating myself up or crying over what I just did. It’s more just this incredibly heavy, sluggish feeling. 

I just kind of sit there, maybe I'll turn on the TV just to have some background noise because, like I said, the house is just so quiet after being around heavy machinery all day, and I feel almost... numb? Or just physically exhausted from the sheer volume of what I just ate. And then I eventually have to drag myself up to throw away the packaging and put the bowls in the sink, and mostly I'm just thinking about how early my alarm is going to go off the next morning. I have to be up at 4:30 AM to get to the site before the first crews arrive, make sure the gates are unlocked, check the overnight weather impacts... it never stops. So I don't really have the energy to sit there wallowing in guilt. I mostly just feel incredibly full, maybe a little annoyed that I made a mess in the kitchen that I now have to deal with, and then I just want to go to bed. So, yeah, I haven't really felt that classic "oh no, what have I done" guilty feeling. I just feel completely done for the day.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating when you're having one of these episodes?

Control... no. Honestly, no, I don't. That’s actually the part that frustrates me the most about all of this. Because, like I was saying earlier, my entire job is about control, right? I control the project schedules, I direct the trades, I manage the material deliveries. If I tell a crew they need to relocate a piece of heavy machinery, it happens. I am so used to being the one calling the shots and keeping everything on track. 

But when I get home and this happens... it’s completely the opposite. Once I start eating on those evenings, it feels like I’m just totally on autopilot. It’s the weirdest thing. I’ll be standing there in the kitchen, maybe I just finished that leftover takeout, and I’ll actually be having this whole rational conversation with myself in my head. I'll be looking right at the clock on the stove, literally telling myself to stop. I'll think, "Okay, that's enough, you have an early crew start tomorrow, you need to be up at 4:30 to unlock the gates, you need to just go to bed." I know how important it is for me to be sharp on site, because if I'm dragging, safety protocols get missed and people can actually get hurt. 

So I know all of that, and I'll maybe even force myself to walk away from the counter and go sit on the couch. But then... it doesn't even matter. It's like I'm not even making a conscious decision anymore. I just find myself getting right back up and going back to the kitchen for more. I’ll open the pantry again, pull out a box of crackers or whatever is sitting there, and just keep going. It’s this bizarre disconnect where my logical brain is practically begging me to stop and go to sleep because of work, but my body is just completely ignoring it and I just keep eating. I really don't feel like I have any say in the matter once that switch flips.
Do you feel like you're eating really fast during these episodes?

Fast? Um... well, I haven't really noticed if I'm eating particularly fast, to be honest. I mean, I guess I'm not really paying attention to the speed of it all when it's happening. Like I was saying, it's just this weird autopilot thing. It's not like I'm standing there shoveling it in as fast as humanly possible like it's a hot dog eating contest or something, but I'm also not, you know, savoring every bite like I'm at some fancy five-star restaurant. 

When I think about eating fast, I think about lunch on the job site. Now *that* is fast. I get maybe fifteen minutes, twenty if I'm lucky, to scarf down a sandwich while I'm sitting in the cab of my truck, usually with my phone pinned between my ear and my shoulder trying to track down where the drywall delivery is, because it was supposed to be there at 10 AM and it's noon. I'm literally chewing as fast as I can just to get some calories in me before the plumbers need me to sign off on a change order. So compared to that... I don't know. 

When I'm at home, in the kitchen at night, it's just... steady, I guess? I'm just eating, and then eating something else, and then something else. I'm not really timing myself or noticing if I'm chewing quickly. I'm usually just staring off into space or looking at the tile backsplash that I really need to re-grout one of these days—which is a whole other project I don't have the energy for right now. But yeah, the actual speed of the eating? I just haven't really paid attention to whether it's unusually fast or not. It just feels like a continuous process until I'm finally too full to keep going.
Have you noticed a decrease in interest in activities you used to enjoy?

Interest in things I used to enjoy... um, no, not really. I mean, I still do the things I usually do. I'm not sitting around staring at the wall all weekend, you know? It's just that my schedule is so packed, I don't really have a ton of free time to begin with. 

When you work construction, especially as a supervisor, your life kind of revolves around the site. I'm up before dawn, I'm dealing with subs, I'm managing materials, I'm putting out fires—sometimes literally, if the welders aren't paying attention—all day long. By the time Saturday rolls around, I'm mostly just trying to catch up on sleep or do my laundry. But I still like doing the things I always liked. I still enjoy going to the hardware store on a Sunday morning. I know that sounds like work, but I actually really like wandering the aisles at Home Depot with a coffee, just looking at the new tools or the different grades of lumber without anyone yelling my name or asking me to approve a timecard. It's peaceful. 

And I still try to get out to the lake when the weather is good. I have this little kayak I bought a few years ago, and I love taking it out. The water is just so quiet compared to the noise of the excavators and the nail guns. I haven't been out as much this season, but that's mostly because we've had so much rain and it's thrown all my pouring schedules completely out of whack, so I've had to work a lot of weekends just to keep the client from breathing down my neck. But the desire to go is still there. I still want to be out on the water. 

So, yeah, I wouldn't say I've lost interest. I just don't always have the time or the physical energy to do stuff, because I'm just so drained from work. But when I do have a minute to breathe, I still enjoy my downtime just as much as I always did. I haven't noticed any kind of drop-off in wanting to do things, if that makes sense.
Do you consider these episodes of eating a lot to be binge eating?

Binge eating... um, I don't know. I mean, I guess it depends on what you actually consider a binge, right? Like, when I hear that word, I think of someone who is just completely out of their mind, eating everything in sight until they're physically sick. Or like, people on those talk shows who have mountains of fast food wrappers around them. And that's not really me. 

But then again, I am eating a lot, and like I said, I feel totally out of control when it happens. It's just... I don't know if I'd use that specific word for it. It feels more like a habit that just gets way out of hand. Like, I get home from the site, and my boots are covered in mud, my ears are ringing from the saws, and I'm just so stressed out from dealing with the general contractor all day. I walk into the house, and it's quiet, and I just start eating to kind of decompress, I guess. And then it just keeps going. 

I don't really sit down and plan to eat a massive amount of food. It's not like I'm stopping at the grocery store on the way home and buying a cart full of junk food with this grand plan to go home and gorge myself. It's more like I just start eating whatever is there, and then I can't stop. I'll have the leftover takeout, then maybe some crackers, then I'll find a box of cereal and eat half of that straight from the box while I'm standing there looking at the fridge. It's a lot of food, definitely more than a normal person would eat for dinner, and I do feel uncomfortably full afterwards. But "binge" just sounds so... extreme. It sounds like a medical term or something. 

So, I don't know if I'd call it that. I just know it's a problem, and I hate that I do it. But trying to put a label on it? I'm really not sure. I guess that's kind of why I'm here, to figure out what exactly is going on with me, because whatever you want to call it, it's definitely not normal and it's really starting to mess with my head.
How often do these episodes of eating a lot happen?

How often? Well, let me think about that for a second, because it’s not exactly like clockwork, you know? It’s not like I have it penned into my calendar next to the concrete pour on Tuesday and the framing inspection on Thursday. It really kind of fluctuates depending on what’s going on at the site and how stressed out I am. 

But if I really sit down and look back over the last few months, trying to average it all out... the whole pattern of it—the eating way too much and then, you know, getting rid of it afterwards, the purging part—it probably averages out to about once a week. 

Now, that doesn't mean it's exactly every seven days. Some weeks are just absolute nightmares. Like, if we get a bad batch of lumber and I have to spend three days arguing with the supplier while the framing crew is just standing around on the clock, my stress levels are through the roof. During a week like that, I might end up doing this whole routine twice. I’ll get home, I’m exhausted, I’m furious, and I just lose it in the kitchen on Tuesday, and then maybe again on Thursday because the problem still isn't fixed. 

But then there are other weeks where things actually go right. The weather holds, the subs show up on time and sober, the client is happy, and I get home feeling like I actually accomplished something instead of just putting out fires all day. On those weeks, I might not do it at all. I might just come home, have a normal dinner, watch some TV, and go to bed. 

So it really bounces around. But yeah, if you take the really bad weeks and the good weeks and just kind of mash them together over the last three or four months, I'd say it averages out to about weekly. It's just... it's always kind of lurking there in the background, you know? Like, I never know if tonight is going to be the night it happens again until I'm actually standing in the kitchen.

Yeah, um... getting rid of it. God, it’s honestly really hard to say out loud, because it just sounds so crazy when I actually hear myself talk about it. But... well, when I realize how much I’ve just eaten, when I’m standing there in my kitchen looking at the empty containers or whatever, this massive wave of panic just hits me. It’s like a physical weight on my chest. 

Because, you know, I work in a really tough industry. Being a female supervisor on a construction site, you are under a microscope every single second of the day. The guys are always looking for a reason to not take you seriously. So I have to command respect. I have to look sharp, tough, but professional. I put so much effort into maintaining this image, this total control over myself, and I work really hard to stay fit and look put-together. 

So after one of those nights where I just completely lose control and eat everything in sight, I start freaking out. I just panic about undoing all the work I’ve put into looking put-together. I start thinking about how I'm going to look in my clothes the next day, if I'm going to look bloated or sloppy, and the anxiety just spirals. 

So... a few times a month, when that panic just gets too loud to ignore, I end up going into the bathroom. I lock the door—even though I live alone, which is ridiculous, I know, but it just feels like this shameful secret—and I make myself throw up. 

It’s awful. I absolutely hate doing it. I’ll be kneeling there on the cold tile, and my knees are already aching from walking the concrete slabs on the site all day, and I’m just thinking to myself, "What on earth are you doing? You’re a grown woman, you have a bachelor's degree, you're running multi-million dollar commercial builds, and here you are hunched over a toilet." It makes me feel so pathetic. But in that specific moment, the fear of what all that food is going to do to my body, the fear of losing that polished, put-together armor I wear to work... it just overrides everything else. I just feel like I have to get it out of my system so I can wake up the next morning, strap my boots on, and pretend I have my life completely under control. So... yeah.
